items.label: f02-sparse-array
items.front: On a 3-item watchlist, `watchlist[99] = "Heat"` runs. What are the length and the contents of the gap?
items.back: length becomes 100 and indexes 3..98 are empty holes (sparse array); loops over length then visit 96 undefined slots.

items.label: f03-mutating-inside-map
items.front: `const out = []; movies.map(m => out.push(m.title));` works, but review flags it. What is wrong?
items.back: map is used for a side effect: it builds and discards an array of push return values (lengths). Return the transformed value instead: `const out = movies.map(m => m.title)`.

items.label: f01-switch-fallthrough
items.front: A switch on ticket status has `case "open": label = "New";` with no break, followed by `case "in_progress": label = "Being worked on"; break;`. Open tickets show "Being worked on". Why?
items.back: Fallthrough: without break, execution continues into the next case's statements, overwriting the label. Add break (or return) at the end of each case.

items.label: f04-block-scope-reference-error
items.front: In `run()`, `blockScoped` is declared with let inside `if (true) { ... }` and logged after the block closes. What happens, and what would var have done?
items.back: ReferenceError: let/const live only in their block. With var the variable is function-scoped, so the log would print 42 — the leak the lesson calls dangerous.

choices.text: true, because find only reports whether any element matched the predicate, like some
Only The Matrix object, since find stops at the first match; filter returns all watched movies
Inception, because find scans from the end of the array toward the start and stops at a match
An array with The Matrix and Inception, because find returns all matches when more than one exists

items.explanation: find returns one element (or undefined). The lesson warns: using find when you need all matches — use filter.

NaN, because count is reset to undefined once createCounter has finished and returned
3, because both counters share the single count variable declared inside createCounter
0, because b has not been incremented yet and returns the value from before the ++

items.prompt: The total is refactored to `movies.reduce((sum, m) => sum + m.minutes)` with the `, 0` removed (and no filter). What value comes out?

choices.text: 303, since the first element is used as the start value and its own minutes are skipped
439, since reduce quietly defaults the accumulator to 0 when no initial value is given
NaN, since the accumulator starts as undefined, and undefined + 155 is not a number
A string like "[object Object]155148": the first movie object becomes the accumulator

choices: 303, since the first element is used as the start value and its own minutes are skipped

NaN, since the accumulator starts as undefined, and undefined + 155 is not a number

items.explanation: Without an initial value, reduce uses element 0 (the whole Matrix object) as the accumulator. The lesson: forgetting the initial value gives the first element as initial — bugs.

choices.text: An empty array: the status check throws and catch recovers, hiding an outage behind an empty list
undefined, because returning a value from inside a catch block is ignored in an async function
The parsed 500 error body, because fetch resolves on any status and json() still runs
A rejected promise with HTTP 500, since the error thrown inside try propagates past the catch block

items.prompt: Someone rewrites the loop as `for (let i = 0; i <= watchlist.length; i++) console.log(i, watchlist[i])`. What changes in the output?

choices.text: It throws a RangeError as soon as the index reaches the length of the array
One extra iteration logs index length with undefined, since valid indexes stop at length - 1
The first element is skipped, because a <= condition makes the loop start counting from index 1
Nothing changes: the engine clamps an out-of-range index to the last valid element

choices: It throws a RangeError as soon as the index reaches the length of the array
One extra iteration logs index length with undefined, since valid indexes stop at length - 1
The first element is skipped, because a <= condition makes the loop start counting from index 1
Nothing changes: the engine clamps an out-of-range index to the last valid element

items.explanation: Arrays are zero-based; reading one past the end is not an error in JS, it just yields undefined. This is the lesson's off-by-one mistake (`<= length`).

items.prompt: In the rating recommendation, `rating` is changed from 6.8 to exactly 8. Which string is chosen?

choices.text: "Worth it", because 8 is not strictly above the threshold and so falls into the middle band
"Skip", because a nested ternary evaluates its last branch whenever both conditions are true
"Must watch": the first test uses >=, so 8 satisfies it and the inner ternary never runs
A SyntaxError, because chained ternaries need parentheses around the inner ternary expression

choices: "Worth it", because 8 is not strictly above the threshold and so falls into the middle band

"Must watch": the first test uses >=, so 8 satisfies it and the inner ternary never runs

items.explanation: Ternaries are evaluated left to right; `rating >= 8` is true for 8, so its branch is the value of the whole expression.

Zero times until the result is read, because every is evaluated lazily on access

It throws a TypeError, because `t.status` is compared against strings that do not include "rejected"
undefined: an if/else-if chain with no matching branch returns nothing, so the label is blank
